item.title: Daughters and Disciples: The Expansive Calling of Women in Christ’s Church
item.description: by Katie Polski
item.content:encoded:
by Katie Polski

Admittedly, I tend to be an optimist. I’m a glass-half-full, “look at this from a different angle” kind of person. I know that can be annoying at times, especially to my more pragmatic friends.

So when I recently read yet another article on women’s limitations in ministry, I let out an audible (and admittedly overdramatic) sigh.

Look, I understand the conversations about women’s roles in the church run deep. As a pastor’s daughter, a pastor’s wife, a seminary graduate, and a full-time church staff member, I know the topic is nuanced and important. Very important.

But…can we also look at it from a different angle?

When conversations about women in the church arise, the question often becomes: What can’t women do? And we tend to settle there. But perhaps that question itself is too small.

I regularly interact with female seminary students and aspiring ministry leaders, and many are pessimistic about finding a place to serve in the PCA. I understand why. I know many feel they are swimming against a cultural climate that often questions women serving in meaningful leadership roles.

But time and again, I offer them a different story – a more optimistic view. There are pastors and elders across our denomination who deeply value women’s gifts, theological training, wisdom, and leadership. I have met them. I serve alongside them. They exist.

More than that, within a confessional Reformed framework, the church offers women not a narrow hallway but a wide field of meaningful, mission-critical work.

The Biblical Pattern: From the Beginning, Co-Laborers

The vision is not a modern accommodation. It’s biblical.

From the beginning, in Gen. 1-2, Adam and Eve bear God’s image together, and they are commissioned to cultivate and steward creation side by side. From the beginning, there is both order and partnership—distinct callings, yet shared participation in God’s work.

In the New Testament, women are named, commended, and entrusted. Romans 16 alone lists women who were foundational participants in ministry. And in the book of Acts, Priscilla instructs and ministers alongside her husband, Aquila. Lydia opens her home as the birthplace of a church in Philippi.

And we shouldn’t overlook the significance of the fact that in all four gospels, women were the first witnesses of the resurrection. In the first century, women were generally not considered reliable or credible witnesses, and their testimony was often discounted. And yet…Jesus entrusts the announcement of his victory to them, appearing to them first.

The pattern we see isn’t silence and sidelining but participation and partnership. Ordered, yes, but also vibrant and significant. As a confessional denomination, the PCA seeks to order its life according to these biblical patterns.

What the PCA Affirms (and Why That Matters)

The polity of the PCA recognizes two ordinary and perpetual offices – elder and deacon – with elders exercising spiritual oversight and governance and deacons overseeing ministries of service. In keeping with its understanding of Scripture, these ordained offices are reserved for qualified men.

The conviction grows from a desire to submit faithfully to Scripture, not from a desire to diminish the gifts or calling of women in Christ’s church. But here is where an important distinction helps us think clearly: Office is not the same as ministry. And ordination is not the same as usefulness.

Much of the ministry described in the New Testament is not office-based but gift-based and Spirit-empowered among the whole body (Rom. 12; 1 Cor. 12; Eph. 4). The formal offices of elder and deacon are vital to the church’s order and health. But when we open Acts and the Epistles, we quickly discover that the life of the early church was not sustained by these offices alone. It was sustained by the saints as a whole.

House churches were hosted and organized by lay believers, many of whom were women. The week-by-week spread of the gospel happened through conversation, hospitality, prayer, generosity, teaching, encouragement, and witness.

While elders carry particular responsibility for authoritative teaching and oversight, much of the ministry described in the New Testament is not tied to ordination. If we begin to equate “real ministry” with the ordained office only, then the opportunities will seem small. But if we let the New Testament shape our understanding, the field expands dramatically.

The Vast “Yes”: Where Women’s Callings Flourish

Here’s what’s significant - the kingdom of God advances not only through pulpits and presbyteries, but also through the daily ministry of the whole church. This happens around dinner tables, through careful theological study, trained counseling, mentoring relationships, through music and liturgy, and through persistent prayer. These are all places where women are and should be using their giftedness.

Do you see how wide the field is?

If God has called you to ministry, it is both a humbling yet great calling, and there are countless places where women are needed.

Theological Depth and Teaching

We need women willing to go deeper in their theological study. My own seminary education was one of the most stretching and rewarding experiences of my life. We need women who study Scripture seriously, who teach other women and children faithfully, who lead Bible studies well, who write thoughtfully, and who mentor intentionally. Theological literacy in the church does not grow accidentally. Women play a vital role in cultivating it.

Worship and Formation

As a worship director, one of my greatest joys is serving alongside pastors to shape the liturgy and music of the church. There are many gifted women who are needed to help plan services. We need female leaders to train musicians in what it means to lead worship, and we need women to continue to shape the doctrinal vocabulary of the church by writing or introducing solid, theologically sound music.

Mercy and Mission

Mercy ministry is not reserved for ordained leaders alone. We need women to be engaged in community outreach, counseling, and discipleship. About half of every church is female, and many of these women long for wise, trained female counsel.

Spiritual Motherhood

The church desperately needs women who are willing to engage in intergenerational discipleship. Whether through structured mentoring or informal rhythms of prayer and presence, women are uniquely positioned to cultivate spiritual maturity in other women (Titus 2).

None of these are “secondary” contributions. They are kingdom-advancing and church-shaping callings. A healthy confessional church should be the safest and richest place for a woman to grow and serve.

A Vision Forward: Cultivating a Culture of Optimism

Just a brief encouragement to my brothers who serve faithfully in our churches. If we want women to flourish in ministry, intentionality matters.

Invite women into theological conversations. Ask women on your staff to attend General Assembly. Encourage formal training and create visible pathways for service. And for the women serving in your midst – whether in an official or unofficial capacity—a word of gratitude goes a long way in reminding them they are seen and their work is valued.

If the next generation of female church leaders only hears the “no,” we have failed to sing out the fullness of the “yes” that Scripture itself celebrates.

God’s church is a household full of meaningful labor. I’m deeply encouraged by the many women in the PCA who are not waiting on the sidelines but who are already building, teaching, singing, discipling, and strengthening Christ’s bride.

I’m grateful for Scripture – for its clarity, order, and its beauty. And I’m grateful for the expansive mercy of God, who calls both men and women to serve in his church. The field is wide, the harvest is plentiful, and there is joyful work to be done for sons and daughters alike.

Katie is a writer, Bible teacher, and speaker. She is married to Chris, a pastor at Trinity Church in St. Louis, MO, and is a mother to three wonderful kids and one wonderful son-in-law. Katie works as the Director of Music Ministries and Special Events at Trinity and writes for several Christian ministries and organizations. She received her Master of Arts in Theology from Covenant Seminary in St. Louis and is author of Beyond the Back Row: Rediscovering the Beauty of the Local Church for your Family and You are a Child of God.

item.title: Encouragement for the Sowers
item.description: We plant and water, but only God can bring the growth.
item.content:encoded:
By Christine Gordon

I didn’t even notice them the first time I walked to the shed. We’d finally had our last spring freeze and I was eager to put summer flower bulbs in the ground before the rains began. I scurried into the gray shed in the corner of my yard, passing the redbud with its lovely dark pink flowers on my left. As I twirled around with a shovel in one hand and gloves in the other, I finally saw them. Three peony stems had pushed themselves up through the ground and reached a height of six or seven inches. They sat quietly beneath the redbud tree, camouflaged by the surrounding grass and dirt.

I’d planted the peonies in early spring the year before. They were in a part of the yard that lacked good soil, so their survival was questionable. I surrounded the bulbs with better soil and fertilizer, watered them faithfully, and checked on them like a new mother. They were blooming when I bought them and struggled to stay green in the Midwest summer heat. I enjoyed their sweet smell and delicate layers while they lasted and hoped the next year they’d last longer. Then I promptly forgot about them.

Paul wrote to the saints in Corinth with a concern for their disunity in 1 Corinthians 3. Apparently, those in the church were giving their loyalty to Paul, Apollos, or other leaders instead of being united under loyalty to Christ. Paul describes his preaching of the gospel and Apollos’s training of the young Christians in verses six and seven: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.” The workers were necessary but not sufficient for the growth of the fragile plants, the new believers. Only God could transform dry seeds into new, green plants.

First-century farmers were acutely aware of their minimal part in the growth of their crops. Of course they prepared the soil and paid attention to the weather. But compared to the power of God, their own agency in crop production was quite limited. Farmers now enjoy specialized tractors and high-tech fertilizers. And yet, still only God can make a seed sprout and grow.

The surprising thing? He does just that.

Just as Paul planted the seed of the gospel in the hearts of the Corinthians, so we plant seeds now. And God faithfully grows them. We plant gospel seeds in the hearts of our friends when we share a sermon that encouraged us. We sow in the soil of our co-workers and neighbors when we tell them what we believe about the cross. We plant seeds in our brothers and sisters at church when we teach first-grade Sunday school to busy little bodies. And God does something mysterious with our efforts that only he can do—he brings growth.

Calvin comments on the work of pastors in their preaching: “... after casting the seed into the ground, they [ministers] give help to the earth as much as is in their power, until it bring forth what it has conceived: but as for making their labor actually productive, that is a miracle of divine grace -- not a work of human industry.” If this is true, the preacher’s part is to faithfully sow the seed and trust God to do his work of growth. The same is true for all of us who teach and share God’s word. We plant and we trust. We sow and we wait. We’re not told which seeds will sprout or which soil the seed will land in (Mark 4:1-20). We’re told that God is faithful to grow his little plants.

Jesus speaks of seed and its growth in Mark 4:26-29: And he said, “The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” The man sows the seed, then sleeps. Why? Because he can’t do more than that. Once he’s done sowing, he must trust God to do the growing. We teach our children that Jesus died for their sins and rose again. Then we wait. We pray. We hope. But only God by his Holy Spirit can take that seed of gospel truth and turn it into something that grows into faith in their hearts. We explain to our neighbor that they are made in the image of God and are valuable and precious because of his care for them. Then we trust that while we sleep and rise, sleep and rise, God will do his work of growing the seed we sowed.

But how does the growth happen? Jesus says the sower doesn’t know.

“He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how.” The sower does his job and goes to bed. While he sleeps, the seed sprouts. The sower wakes up, lives through another day, and the tiny sprout grows. All of this happens without the knowledge or help of the sower.

Which brings me back to my peonies.

I planted and watered them, sure. But then I forgot about them. Fall rains came and went. Winter ice storms covered the ground. Spring sun warmed the soil, and God made them grow. Their ugly, twisted stems (have you seen peony stems?) will grow into the most delicately layered flowers in the garden.

You may not know if your child hears the gospel truth you tell them when they’re hurting. Tell them anyway. Plant the seed of God’s word and trust him to grow it. You may not know if the Christian book you shared with your neighbor will make any difference in their life. Give it to them anyway. Parents, pastors, and Sunday school teachers, neighbors and friends who work and hope for growth in the kingdom: Trust that the one who wrote the word will grow the seed. Sleep and rise, work and play. Forget where you’ve planted, plant in new soils. God will do his secret work of growing his little plants, and one day when you’ve forgotten your meager efforts, God, the perfect gardener, may surprise you with beautiful new growth in the heart of your neighbor.

Christine Gordon (MATS, Covenant Theological Seminary) is wife to Michael and mother of three. She is the cofounder of At His Feet Studies and a visiting instructor at Covenant Theological Seminary.

item.title: Who Will Fill the Pulpits?
item.description: Ligon Duncan, Tom Gibbs, and Derek Radney on the PCA’s coming pastoral shortage
item.content:encoded:
The PCA is approaching an important long-term question: How will the denomination raise up enough qualified pastors to serve its churches, plant new ones, and lead growing ministries in the decades ahead? A large generation of pastors is nearing retirement, the PCA continues to grow, and RUF and other ministries are expanding into new places. At the same time, fewer young men are imagining pastoral ministry as a possible vocation, financial barriers can make seminary difficult to pursue, and pastors are leaving pulpits because of burnout, early retirement, and other pressures.

These converging factors raise questions about the entire pastoral pipeline—from identifying and encouraging potential ministers to training, supporting, and placing them well. That work cannot belong to seminaries alone. It requires local churches, presbyteries, campus ministries, seminaries, and the wider denomination to see themselves as partners in raising up the next generation.

In this conversation, Derek Radney speaks with seminary presidents Ligon Duncan and Tom Gibbs about the challenges and opportunities ahead—and how the whole church can work together to prepare pastors for a lifetime of faithful ministry.

item.title: Ministry—Theological Vision Part Ten
item.description: By Geoff Bradford
item.content:encoded:
By Geoff Bradford

A Culture of Equipping

Perhaps the greatest challenge facing the PCA is not deciding who may do which task. It is becoming churches where every member actually ministers. Many congregations affirm the priesthood of all believers while functioning as though ministry belongs almost entirely to paid staff. Others rightly emphasize participation but unintentionally diminish the unique responsibility Christ has entrusted to ordained shepherds. AMR envisions something better:

Imagine churches where elders intentionally identify, encourage, and deploy the gifts of the congregation… Where women disciple younger women with wisdom and theological depth… Where older men invest in younger men… Where deacons mobilize saints for works of mercy… Where members naturally pray with one another, bear burdens, welcome strangers, teach children, encourage the discouraged, and speak gospel truth into everyday life… Where officers rejoice not because they are doing all the ministry but because they are equipping others to do it. Such churches increasingly embody Christ himself.

Contrast this vision with our cultural moment. The American church is in a time of cultural change. This reckoning with abuses of leadership in our past and present has in some cases led to healthy and helpful calls for repentance, a “deconstruction” of ministries that were harmful. Yet in other contexts, it has led others to destruction: a rejection of the church entirely or a dismantling of Biblical structures and doctrines. Thus the American church today is tempted toward two opposite and unbiblical overreactions: a temptation to flatten Christ’s ordered offices in the name of equality; a second to elevate ordained office in a way that minimizes the ministry Christ intends for every believer.

The Poverty of Clericalism vs. the General Office of Every Believer

One of the striking features of the New Testament is how much ministry belongs to ordinary Christians. This has often been called the “General Office of every believer”—the Reformed way of describing the priesthood of all believers and the shared ministry entrusted to every Christian. When Paul describes the church, he rarely pictures a congregation gathered around a few gifted leaders while everyone else watches. Instead, he speaks of a body “joined and held together by every joint” that “when each part is working properly, makes the body grow” (Eph. 4:16). Peter tells believers to use whatever gifts they have received to serve one another as faithful stewards of God’s grace (1 Pet. 4:10). Paul urges the Corinthians to pursue spiritual gifts “for building up the church” (1 Cor. 14:12). The New Testament envisions a congregation alive with mutual ministry.

Yet this flourishing does not happen apart from leadership. Christ “gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers” for a purpose: “to equip the saints for the work of ministry” (Eph. 4:11–12). The ministry belongs to the whole church because Christ first gives shepherds to prepare his people for that ministry.

This conviction lies behind AMR’s theological vision:

“Because, through his elders, Christ the Overseer of our souls equips his people to participate in this mission and to build each other up into a community that increasingly embodies him, we commit to structures of ministry that encourage among all members the godly exercise of spiritual gifts…”

The order is important: Christ builds his church by giving ordained shepherds who equip the saints for the work of ministry. But those shepherds are not the church’s only ministers! Their calling is to cultivate a congregation in which every member—men and women alike—increasingly speaks the truth in love, bears one another’s burdens, admonishes, encourages, serves, teaches appropriately, shows mercy, practices hospitality, and exercises every gift Christ has supplied.

Every generation of the church faces the temptation toward clericalism. Clericalism assumes that meaningful ministry belongs primarily to ordained officers while everyone else becomes a spectator. Ministry becomes something performed by professionals rather than shared throughout the body. It is antithetical to our Biblical convictions and our Reformed history.

This temptation has appeared in many forms throughout church history. Sometimes it has elevated clergy into a spiritual class distinct from ordinary believers. Sometimes it has unintentionally developed through church culture, where members assume that discipleship, counseling, evangelism, visitation, mercy ministry, and spiritual encouragement are primarily the pastor’s responsibility.

The Westminster Standards point us in another direction. Christ has indeed established ordained offices for the government, teaching, and oversight of his church. Yet all believers share in Christ’s anointing, offering spiritual sacrifices and confessing his name before the world (WLC 63; WCF 26). The ministry of the church is never exhausted by the ministry of its officers.

Healthy Presbyterian churches have always understood this! Some of the most transformative ministry happens around dinner tables, in community groups, in hospital rooms, over coffee after worship, in youth discipleship, children’s ministry, mercy ministry, neighborhood evangelism, and quiet conversations where believers patiently apply God’s Word to one another’s lives. When elders faithfully equip the saints, the whole body grows.

The Poverty of Egalitarianism vs. the Goodness of Ordered Ministry

If clericalism diminishes the ministry of the congregation, egalitarianism obscures the distinct offices Christ himself has given to his church. Affirming the ministry of every believer does not eliminate Christ’s distinct offices. Scripture simultaneously expands ministry to the whole church and preserves ordained leadership.

The New Testament does not oppose authority to participation. Rather, it joins them together. Christ appoints elders precisely so that the whole church might flourish.

Presbyterians have long confessed that Christ governs his church through ordained elders who exercise spiritual oversight under the authority of Scripture. This ordering is not a reflection of cultural preference or human hierarchy but of Christ’s wisdom for the health of his people. For that reason, AMR rightly opposes “an egalitarianism that eradicates the order ordained by Christ.”

This statement should not be understood negatively, as though the primary concern is preserving boundaries. Rather, it is profoundly positive and seeks to protect a God-given good.

Because Scripture roots the office of elder in creation rather than merely church pragmatics or cultural norms, AMR understands the church’s ordered ministry to reflect—not erase—the goodness of sexual difference. Egalitarianism flattens out the Biblical gift of gender, treating sexual difference as irrelevant to Christ’s ordering of the church. Yet Scripture teaches that there is inherent glory in being a man and inherent glory in being a woman. These differences are not obstacles to ministry but gifts to be received with gratitude. Men and women together share in the General Office of the church, while Scripture also preserves distinct responsibilities within Christ’s ordered church.

Christ gives ordained leadership because he loves his church. It is not a historical mistake, but a timeless gift. Just as the body requires both bones and muscles—structure and movement—so the church flourishes when shepherds faithfully shepherd and every member faithfully ministers.

The question is never whether every believer should participate in ministry; Scripture answers that with a resounding “yes!” The question is how Christ has ordered that ministry for the building up of his church. AMR therefore celebrates both the General Office of every believer and the complementary gifts of men and women as expressions of Christ’s wise ordering of his church.

Speaking the Truth in Love

Ephesians 4 provides the heartbeat of this vision. Christ gives shepherds. Shepherds equip the saints. The saints speak the truth in love. And, as every member does its work, the whole body grows into maturity. This growth is measured not simply by organizational effectiveness but by Christlikeness. The goal is “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13). Mature churches are rich in personal holiness, marked by communal virtue, and equipped with practical wisdom for faithful living in every sphere of life.

That is ultimately why AMR rejects both clericalism and egalitarianism. One suppresses the gifts Christ has given his people; the other disregards the order Christ has established for those gifts to flourish. The risen Christ has provided both gifts and shepherds. We need both! As elders faithfully equip and members faithfully minister, Christ continues his work of building a church that increasingly displays his own life to the world.

TE Geoff Bradford has served as the senior pastor of Christ the King Presbyterian Church in downtown Raleigh, NC since 2011. He is a native of Kingsport, TN, then attended Davidson College, where he met his wife, Susan. Susan is Geoff’s true love and ministry partner. They have raised 6 sons and done a lot of ministry together–at Liberti Church, which they helped plant in Philadelphia, and now at CtK. They love their boys but now also enjoy finally having daughters(in-law) and a granddaughter.

item.title: Elders—Theological Vision Part Nine
item.description: We are continuing to expand and explain AMR’s Theological Vision, offering a closer look at each of its core commitments.
item.content:encoded:
We are continuing to expand and explain AMR’s Theological Vision, offering a closer look at each of its core commitments. as it shapes the church’s pursuit of renewal, faithfulness, and mission amid fear, cynicism, and cultural uncertainty.

by Erik Bonkovsky

“Because, as the gospel creates new church communities, Christ the Chief Shepherd pastors his people through elders,

  • We commit to diligently training and carefully ordaining elders from various languages and cultures whose ministry, rule, and care reflect the strength and gentleness of Christ: godly men whose character is above reproach, exemplary in integrity, humility, and repentance, and whose competence in the Word of God enables them to instruct, correct, and guard against error.

  • We oppose expressions of leadership that either abdicate authority or exercise it in a domineering and abusive manner.”

    (from the AMR Theological Vision)

During my time in seminary in the late 1990s, I first experienced what it means to be shepherded by the elders of a local church. A faithful ruling elder regularly called me, asking how he might pray for me. He invited me out for dinner, asking questions about both my studies and my soul. At weekly worship he made a point to greet me, often following up on the issues we had talked about earlier. Initially, I didn’t have a category for what he was doing. But now I see that he was teaching me—a future pastor—that Christ the Chief Shepherd pastors his people through Christ-shaped elders.

Although I grew up in a church-attending family, I’d never been cared for like that by someone who wasn’t a “professional Christian.” Sure, pastors shook my hand in the receiving line after the service. Campus ministry staff met with me regularly to disciple me. The college pastor at my church gave me books to read and asked me how I was growing in godliness and prayer. But here was an adult man, with a busy job and a family of his own, pastoring me with patience and grace.

Now having served as a local church pastor for the last twenty years I understand the indispensability of Christ-shaped elders in sustaining the body of Christ. The elders of the church are not a Board of Directors carrying out administrative responsibilities. The elders are not solely successful business leaders shouldering the financial burdens of the church. They are pastors, elders, teachers, shepherds. They’re given a variety of titles to represent the variety of functions carried out within the church. And recognizing that God does not look on the outward appearance but on the heart (1 Samuel 16: 7), they are leaders shaped not by the outward standards of the world but by the inward standards of character, piety, and faithfulness.

A Commitment to Elder Training

What I didn’t see in that elder’s predictable, humble care for me during seminary was the diligent training and careful ordination process he had undergone in order to prepare him to minister to me. Elders don’t emerge in the church fully formed; they are developed, they are grown in a greenhouse of grace, fed by the Word and sustained by the Spirit. This is true of both ruling elders and teaching elders. The development of Christ-shaped elders comes through both informal and formal means. And the development of Christ-shaped elders manifests not only in their theological orthodoxy (right belief), but also in a corresponding orthopraxy (right living), and orthopathy (right feeling). Christ-shaped elders are whole in mind, body, and heart—men with intellectual understanding, spiritual maturity, and emotional health.

Thus, perhaps more than anything, Christ-shaped elders are formed by a habit of repentance. As those who trace our theological heritage back to a door in Wittenberg must heed the first of Luther’s 95 theses: “Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ, when He said, ‘Repent,’ willed that the whole life of believers should be repentance.” Church elders are formed by a repentance which roots them in God’s grace and which produces the fruit of holy living in their lives. That’s why I invite the elders of our church to join me as pacesetters in repentance for our congregation. In leading the way in repentance, our congregation over time sees the beauty of God’s free grace for our sin. Furthermore, our regular repentance leads us into dependence on God’s Spirit; the Spirit that produces the fruit of integrity, piety, and faithfulness.

Through God’s Varied Grace

Although all elder training in the PCA consists of certain non-negotiables, it can (and should) take many forms across the denomination. Two years ago our church launched an Emerging Leaders Program focused on identifying and nurturing future church leaders. We were partly inspired in this work by a nearby sister church that for many years has run a Pastoral Intern program which has proved successful in guiding seminary-trained men through licensure and ministry preparation. In a year-long program these pastoral interns develop both their facility in teaching and preaching God’s Word and their soul-readiness to lead and serve amidst the vagaries of congregational life. The leadership development programs at our respective churches look different, but are committed to the same goal: forming Christ-shaped elders for the PCA.

At a historical moment when many in the church are concerned about addressing the future leadership pipelines for the church, we need to remember that God sees fit to gift, call, and equip a variety of men for the office of elder. While meeting the same high standards of character and doctrinal understanding, elders—as shepherds—must also know their respective sheep. These local leaders called into specific ministry contexts should represent all sorts of background cultures and languages so that the church can extend to people of every tribe, tongue, and nation.

This summer I’ve been preaching through the book of 1 Peter which has a lot to say about Christ-shaped elders. In chapter 4 Peter writes, “As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of varied grace.” On the basis of God’s varied grace, Christ-shaped leaders should recognize their unique roles within the household of God and seek opportunities to effectively steward their gifts in service to others. Within God’s family there is no place for coveting the gifts God has given to another man, nor expecting that every elder be cast from the exact same mold. A denomination committed to Christ-shaped elders must be receptive to diverse expressions of God’s varied grace.

AMR seeks to cultivate a hospitable posture to this kind of diversity of Christ-shaped elders and emerging leaders within the denomination, particularly those coming from cultural backgrounds outside of what is typical in the PCA. We eschew the temptations of cultural narrowness and contextual familiarity, recognizing that a national denomination requires heterogeneous leadership. Therefore, a hospitable posture starts with an awareness of different experiences within the PCA and a sensitivity to the issues that are of a primary concern to others. Such a posture also avoids maintaining unnecessary barriers to full participation and leadership within the denomination. Christ-shaped elders model the stewardship of authority exhibited by Jesus himself, who willingly disadvantaged himself for the sake of the marginalized and disenfranchised.

Not Domineering

Later, in the same book, Peter gives a warning against flawed leadership in the church. “Shepherd the flock of God that is among you,” he exhorts, “exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you, not for shameful gain, but eagerly, not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.” (1 Peter 5:4)

Christ-shaped elders must avoid all sorts of potential pitfalls in their leadership. In our church’s training classes, we talk through real-life examples (unfortunately, all too common in our denomination) of leadership expressions that deviate from the Biblical standard. We talk about the elders who, mimicking that initial sin of our federal head Adam, abdicate leadership, remaining silent and passive while individuals in the congregation disobey the straightforward teaching of God. We talk about elders who come in wolf’s clothing, seeking to steal, kill, and destroy the vulnerable sheep of God. We talk about those church leaders who, seduced by the trappings of power and authority, use their position to abuse the sheep, speaking and acting harshly, in violation of both Christ’s example and exhortation.

The work of shepherding in Christ’s Church offers temptations too great to resist and pressures too great to bear alone. Fortunately, God uses Christ-shaped elders themselves to guard the church against malformed elders. This guarding initially happens individually, with one brother correcting another, just as I was gently chastened earlier this year by a brother in my presbytery. But it can (and must) also happen through the formal structures of the church’s discipline process. The biblical beauty of presbyterianism is that God in his wisdom provides a plurality of Christ-shaped elders for his church, to share together in the sacred calling of shepherding and to preserve the Christ-likeness of these elders themselves.

Conclusion

Since the New Testament era the Kingdom of God has expanded through the mission of church-planting, which itself has required the multiplication of Christ-shaped elders to lead and pastor those churches. God’s Kingdom will continue to be renewed and expanded through such Christ-shaped elders within the PCA. For my part, in my own little corner of the denomination, I’m trying to follow the pattern that I learned from a faithful ruling elder outside of Philadelphia, twenty-five years ago: showing up, asking questions, sharing from the Word, and praying. May we all do the same.

TE Erik Bonkovsky is the senior pastor at City Church of Richmond in Richmond, VA, a church he planted in 2008. A native New Englander, Erik studied at Princeton University (B.A. in History, 1998), Westminster Seminary (M.Div., 2001), and Covenant Seminary (D.Min., 2017). He lives in Richmond with his wife, Sarah, and their three children.

item.title: Mission—Theological Vision Part Eight
item.description: We are continuing to expand and explain AMR’s Theological Vision, offering a closer look at each of its core commitments.
item.content:encoded:
We are continuing to expand and explain AMR’s Theological Vision, offering a closer look at each of its core commitments. as it shapes the church’s pursuit of renewal, faithfulness, and mission amid fear, cynicism, and cultural uncertainty.

by Tony Wang

John Stott famously described the preacher’s task as bridge-building — standing between two worlds, the world of Scripture and the world of the present, refusing to collapse into either one. Stand only in the biblical world, and the sermon becomes a relic, technically faithful but unintelligible to anyone who doesn’t already speak its language. Stand only in the contemporary world, and the sermon becomes therapeutic noise, fluent in the culture’s idiom but with nothing left to say that the culture didn’t already believe. Stott’s image wasn’t only about preaching; it names the basic posture every ministry of the gospel must take toward its context. The bridge has to reach all the way to both banks, or it isn’t a bridge at all.

This is the tension AMR’s theological vision names when it commits the PCA to Christ-exalting mission:

Because Christ the Apostle enlists his Church as ambassadors of the single gospel of Christ to all,

  • We commit to the work of making disciples, desiring to see the loving rule of Christ take hold of every tongue, tribe, and nation. We believe it is the gospel of Christ alone that can bring this salvation. We also believe that this gospel proclamation must be thoughtfully adapted to its specific context and adorned with the Church’s good works.

  • We oppose any contextualization of the gospel that compromises its message or any extrabiblical restriction that hinders the gospel from taking root in all cultures.

    (from the AMR Theological Vision)

The Church Is Sent by Christ, Not by Culture

Before mission can be rightly contextualized, it must first be rightly located. The Church does not stand at the origin of its own sending. Christ does. He is himself the Apostle — the one sent from the Father into the world (Heb. 3:1) — and it is only because he has first been sent that he can turn to his disciples and say, “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21). Mission, then, is not an initiative the Church takes up on Christ’s behalf; it is a participation in a sending already accomplished, extended now through his body. The Great Commission is not a delegation of tasks to a resourceful institution but a declaration of authority: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore...” (Matt. 28:18–20). The imperative rests entirely on the indicative. We go because he reigns.

This is also why Paul can describe the Church’s task in the audacious language of embassy: “we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us” (2 Cor. 5:18–20). An ambassador does not write his own instructions. He carries another’s message, under ƒanother’s authority, into territory not his own. This is the deep grammar beneath AMR’s confession that Christ “enlists his Church as ambassadors of the single gospel of Christ to all.” Because the message is not ours to originate, it is also not ours to alter. What we are free — indeed obligated — to adapt is how that message meets the particular world before us. What we are never free to adapt is the message itself.

The Gospel Is for Everyone — Which Is Why It Must Be Contextualized

If the gospel belongs to Christ and not to any single culture, then its reach cannot stop at the border of the culture in which it was first understood by us. AMR’s statement envisions the loving rule of Christ taking hold of “every tongue, tribe, and nation” — language drawn from the throne room of Revelation, where the redeemed are not a homogenized mass but a multitude who remain, even in glory, identifiable by tribe and tongue. The gospel does not erase cultural particularity; it travels into it, again and again, without ever becoming permanently at home in any one of them.

Paul’s own ministry displays what this traveling looks like. In the synagogue he reasoned from the Scriptures, assuming a shared framework of covenant and promise. In Athens he started instead from an altar to an unknown god, quoted the city’s own poets, and argued from nature rather than Torah. The starting point changed; the message did not. In both places he proclaimed the same God, the same coming judgment, the same call to repentance, the same Christ raised from the dead. His approach moved toward whoever was listening. His gospel remained captive to the One who sent him.

This has a sobering implication for how we understand our own preaching and practice. There is no such thing as an uncontextualized gospel presentation. Every sermon, every liturgy, every explanation of sin and grace already comes clothed in a particular vocabulary, assumes a particular set of cultural reference points, and answers questions a particular audience is actually asking. The minister who insists he is “just preaching the text,” unadorned by any cultural accommodation” has not escaped contextualization — he has simply contextualized invisibly, to himself, and mistaken his own cultural idiom for the timeless form of the gospel itself. This is a subtler danger than it appears, because it wears the mask of faithfulness. A missionary who refuses to translate Scripture into the language of the people he serves is not being more biblical than the missionary who does; he is simply insisting that his hearers first become fluent in his culture before they may hear of Christ in theirs.

To confess, then, that the gospel must be “thoughtfully adapted to its specific context” is not a concession wrung from a reluctant orthodoxy. It is a corollary of the gospel’s own universality. Precisely because Christ is Lord of every tribe and tongue, and not merely of ours, faithfulness requires the hard, ongoing labor of discerning what in our own proclamation is gospel and what is merely custom — so that the gospel we carry across cultural lines is recognizably the same gospel, and not our accent mistaken for its substance.

The Two Ditches

Every act of contextualization walks a narrow path with a ditch on either side, and the temptation is always to overcorrect away from one danger directly into the other.

The first ditch is overcontextualization. Here the gospel is so thoroughly absorbed into its cultural surroundings that it loses the very edges that made it gospel—good news, and not good advice. A church that overcontextualizes may grow numerically while ceasing, in any meaningful sense, to confront sin, summon repentance, or proclaim a Christ who saves rather than merely affirms. This is the danger we name when we oppose “any contextualization of the gospel that compromises its message.”

The second ditch is undercontextualization. Here the failure runs the opposite direction: cultural forms, assumptions, and preferences—often invisible to those who hold them, because they feel simply like “how church is done”—are bound onto the conscience as though they were biblical requirements. The gospel is rejected, but for the wrong reason. Not because the cross gives offense, but because a foreign culture does. This is the danger we name when we oppose “any extrabiblical restriction that hinders the gospel from taking root in all cultures.”

What holds the path steady between these ditches is not a technique but a theology. The gospel is not a compromise between moralism and license, nor a midpoint between cultural captivity and cultural rigidity; it is something else altogether. That distinction must govern how the gospel is carried into culture. The gospel is neither an infinitely pliable message that bends toward whatever a culture already wants to hear, nor a fixed cultural artifact that requires a people first to become Western, Southern, or Reformed-flavored American before they may receive it. To borrow Tolkien’s imagery, we may rightly love the Shire without mistaking it for the whole of Middle-earth. Our inherited ecclesiastical home may contain real goods worth cherishing and conserving, but Christ’s mission does not end at the borders of what is familiar to us. The gospel has a fixed center and genuinely varied, though never normless, cultural clothing.

This is why contextualization cannot be reduced to a set of techniques for making the gospel more palatable. It is a theological discipline, requiring the same humility and the same conviction that mark faithful biblical interpretation elsewhere—a constant asking of Scripture what is essential to the message and what is merely the accent in which we ourselves first received it. We walk between ditches we did not choose, carrying a gospel we did not invent, trusting the One who sent us to keep our steps.

Adorned with Good Works

Contextualization is not only a matter of vocabulary. If it were, it would be little more than translation—finding the right words in the right language and trusting the work to be done. But the gospel is not merely spoken into a culture; it is meant to be seen there, embodied in a community whose common life bears public witness to the message it proclaims. This is what our statement means in confessing that gospel proclamation must be “adorned with the Church’s good works.” The adornment is not decorative in the sense of optional. It is adornment in the sense that a wedding ring adorns a marriage—visible evidence of a reality the words alone cannot fully display.

Word and deed belong together because the gospel makes claims about the whole of life: about bodies as well as souls, about justice as well as forgiveness, about the reconciliation of persons to God and, flowing from that, to one another. A gospel proclaimed in a community that shows no mercy to the poor, no welcome to the stranger, no reconciliation across old hostilities, is not a fuller gospel merely because its doctrine is precise. It is a gospel whose deeds are testifying against its words. Conversely, deeds of mercy and justice untethered from the proclamation of Christ crucified and risen may accomplish much temporal good, but they cannot accomplish what only the gospel can: the reconciliation of sinners to God through Christ, spoken of plainly and without embarrassment (2 Cor. 5:18–20).

What counts as fitting adornment is itself contextual: a people wounded by exploitation will read economic integrity as gospel evidence; a people fractured by enmity will read reconciled community that way. The forms vary; what remains constant is that every such work points beyond itself, refusing to rest as its own justification, gesturing always toward the Christ it cannot replace.

Conclusion

Stott’s bridge holds only because one bank never moves. Scripture stands fixed, complete, not the bridge-builder’s to alter—while the world on the other side is never the same shore twice, shifting by culture, by generation, by tongue. The PCA must therefore keep building the bridge—not by changing the gospel, but by carrying the same gospel faithfully into each new context. This is finally why contextualization is not a concession to be managed but a calling to be trusted. The gospel we carry across cultural distance is not our own invention, and its journey into every tongue and tribe rests not on our ingenuity but on the authority of the One who sends us. We do not stand at the origin of this mission, and we will not stand at its completion. Between those two points, we labor as ambassadors carrying a message not our own, adorning it with works that testify rather than substitute, until the earth is full of the knowledge of the glory of the Lord as the waters cover the sea. Christ has sent his Church with one gospel for all peoples.

Tony grew up in China and met his wife, Lin, while studying in Canada. He serves as the Lead Pastor of Grace Irvine Church, the PCA’s first Mandarin-speaking congregation on the West Coast. With a background in engineering physics, Tony is passionate about systematic theology, church planting, and equipping leaders for gospel movements. He also co-founded the City Lights Church Planting Network, a ministry dedicated to reaching Chinese immigrants by planting gospel-centered churches.

item.title: Presbyterian—Theological Vision Part Seven
item.description: We are continuing to expand and explain AMR’s Theological Vision, offering a closer look at each of its core commitments.
item.content:encoded:
We are continuing to expand and explain AMR’s Theological Vision, offering a closer look at each of its core commitments. as it shapes the church’s pursuit of renewal, faithfulness, and mission amid fear, cynicism, and cultural uncertainty.

By Sean Michael Lucas

“We make no apology for our determination that this Church will be thoroughly Calvinistic in doctrine and intensely Presbyterian in government”—such was the claim that the first moderator of the Presbyterian Church in America, W. Jack Williamson, made at our first General Assembly. Of course, in the fifty-plus years since the PCA’s founding, we have wrestled with what it means to be “intensely Presbyterian in government.”

What did the founding generation mean by this? They had just experienced the massive centralization of the old Presbyterian Church in the United States, in which the various agency boards were eliminated for the forty-person General Executive Council. They had seen how the General Assembly enforced its will on the lower courts, especially in Mississippi. And they saw how “Union Presbyteries” and “Union Synods” were created by the Assembly to foster a future reunion with the northern Presbyterian Church over the objections of conservatives in the church.

Over against all this centralized power, the founders articulated a principle of “grassroots Presbyterianism.” With this, the main court of the church is the presbytery—the local presbytery is responsible for missions, for nominating men for the higher courts, for credentialing ministers and determining how that would occur. The PCA was structured to put as much power under the local control of presbyteries and away from the Assembly or the committees and agencies—so much so that for the first five years, the various agencies could not have their headquarters in the same city!

Fast Forward to the Present

Now that the PCA has celebrated its fiftieth birthday, it’s fair to ask how that’s worked for us. One of the trends over the past decade has been the centralization of power in the Assembly and with that a new interest in what it means to be “intensely Presbyterian in government.”

AMR’s theological vision statement clearly states that we too believe in being Presbyterian in government.

From the Theological Vision Statement:

Because Christ the King gathers and governs his Church, disciplining his flock through the polity and order he has given,

  • We commit to acting as faithful stewards of the institution we have inherited, diligently pursuing its purity, peace, and unity. We will actively engage in the labors required by its discipline and government, confident that through the orderly processes of Presbyterianism, Christ cares for his Church.

  • We oppose all forms of divisiveness, such as empty proceduralism or mob-like adjudication, instead energetically pursuing the biblical and constitutional means for confronting and correcting fellow believers.

We would suggest that being “intensely” Presbyterian does not mean being divisively or harshly so. The Presbyterian processes in the Book of Church Order, the Rules of Assembly Operation, and Robert’s Rules of Order are meant to honor Christ the King and to serve the Church.

That’s where this article starts. From the earliest days of Presbyterianism—back to John Knox himself—we have stood for Christ’s kingship over his church. He is the one who gathers his church; he is the one who grows his church. Pastors and elders may preach and teach, sowing the seed of Christ’s Word, but God gives the increase (1 Cor 3:7). Above all, the church belongs to Christ—it is God’s field, God’s building (1 Cor 3:9).

But how does Christ rule his church? Through officers and laws. The officers he gives are elders and deacons; they are his gift to the church (Eph 4:8, 11–12). The laws that he gives are the broad outlines of Presbyterian polity—the elements of officers, oversight, and discipline. AMR strongly believes that the elements of our polity are given by Christ and are necessary for the existence of the church (WCF 1:6). There are many other circumstantial things we do with our church’s polity that are necessary for the good order of the church—they are not necessarily revealed in Holy Scripture but are agreeable to those general rules and guidelines.

AMR’s Presbyterian Commitment

We are committed to stewarding this Presbyterian branch of the visible church. The church is a necessary institution for the advancement of God’s mission; denominations form to carry out mission around confessional distinctives. The PCA stands in a long American Presbyterian tradition that we gladly inherit and utilize for the purity, peace, and unity of Christ’s church.

To that end, AMR is committed to being Presbyterian churchmen. What does that mean? It means seeking the good of the entire body—not just our friends, our former seminary classmates, our group. It means trusting the brothers, believing the best about them and their ministries, refusing to gossip about them, preserving their reputations. It means partnering together for mission, both at the regional presbytery level and at the national level. It means supporting denominational committees and agencies because that is how we do mission together.

It also means showing up to presbytery and General Assembly, having prepared to be good presbyters. It means participating on presbytery and Assembly committees, even those that do not seem to be prominent or have much “power” or influence. It means generally staying to the end of the meeting and not using the excuse of a long drive home to leave early.

And above all, our commitment means that we have a fundamental confidence in the goodness of our Presbyterian processes. Not because they are good in themselves, but because through them Christ rules and cares for his church. Christ cares for his church through officers and laws—and while many of our “laws” are manmade, circumstantial, and not divine law, they still are good processes that Christ himself uses for our good and his glory.

AMR’s Presbyterian Concerns

My expectation is that no matter where one finds himself in the PCA landscape, everything thus far would be relatively uncontroversial, even when a bit bracing. But AMR does have concerns about how Presbyterianism can be misused and abused. Because let’s be real: when we all do what we’ve committed to do, Presbyterianism is the best system of church government in the history of the world; but when we don’t do it or when we misuse it, Presbyterianism is the worst.

That’s why we stake our flag here: we oppose all forms of divisiveness from whatever quarter of the church it arises. Divisiveness can look like a Twitter mob trying to take down people or stop events. It can also look like an ever-increasing punctilious proceduralism—which is evidenced in the number of Book of Church Order–amending overtures, Review of Presbytery Records citations, and Standing Judicial Commission cases. In our present day, it appears that our increased litigiousness is not so much “intensely Presbyterian,” but harsh and divisive.

AMR continues to champion our biblical and Presbyterian polity processes. And to be sure, there are appropriate overtures, citations, and judicial cases—those are the processes that we use to perfect our polity and ensure appropriate discipline. But I, for one, am concerned that our present fad of “Presby-maxxing” is, ironically, a move away from our founders’ genius back toward the same centralizing instincts of the old dying church from which the PCA sprang.

Spiritual and missional growth isn’t found in ever-increasing regulation. It is found in the trust that Christ the King of the church engenders among brothers and sisters who are committed to common confessional and missional distinctives.

Born in Stratford, New Jersey, Sean moved up and down the eastern seaboard as a child. He graduated from Bob Jones University (BA, 1993; MA, 1994) and Westminster Theological Seminary (PhD, 2002). He was ordained as a Presbyterian minister in 2003, then served on the pastoral staff of Community Presbyterian Church (PCA), Louisville, Kentucky, and Covenant Presbyterian Church (PCA), St. Louis, Missouri. In 2009, he became Senior Pastor of the First Presbyterian Church, Hattiesburg, Mississippi, where he served until coming to serve as senior pastor at Independent Presbyterian Church, Memphis, Tennessee in 2017.

Sean has taught at two theological seminaries. He is presently the Chancellor’s Professor of Church History at Reformed Theological Seminary, where he has taught since 2011. Prior to that, he was chief academic officer and associate professor of church history at Covenant Theological Seminary, where he served from 2004 to 2009.

Sean has also written many books, including On Being Presbyterian: Our Beliefs, Practices, and Stories (2006); God’s Grand Design: The Theological Vision of Jonathan Edwards (2011); J. Gresham Machen (2015); and For a Continuing Church: The Roots of the Presbyterian Church in America (2015). He and his wife Sara have four adult children: Samuel, Elizabeth, Andrew, and Benjamin.

item.title: Parsing a Passing Distinction
item.description: by Chuck Colson
item.content:encoded:
by Chuck Colson

After a narrow loss at last year’s General Assembly, a new round of overtures has appeared for 2026 seeking to restrict who can distribute the elements of the Lord’s Supper to the congregation (Overtures 31 and 60). Due to ambiguity around what it means to distribute, the overtures distinguish what it means “to serve” the elements from what it means “to pass” the elements. The overall aim of the overtures is to restrict non-ordained officers from participating in serving the elements. Overture 31 restricts the distribution to ordained ruling elders; Overture 60 restricts it to ordained officers.

There are several issues in these overtures that deserve scrutiny; however, for the sake of brevity, I’ll focus on the proposed distinction between “serving” and “merely passing” the elements.

Distributing the Elements

In the PCA, a variety of methods are used to distribute the elements, complicating any attempt to distinguish between “serving” and “merely passing” them. Consider the following four common patterns of distribution found across our denomination:

  • Dine-in—believers come forward to sit at a table where the elements are distributed among them. In a few congregations, believers come forward to kneel at an altar rail where the elements are distributed to them.

  • Drive-thru—believers come forward to be served at a station where they receive the elements, along with a spoken word regarding the sacrament (The body of our Lord Jesus Christ which was broken for you / the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ which was shed for you), and consume the elements at the station.

  • Takeout—believers come forward to pick up the elements, either from a person or a table, and return to their seats to take the elements in unison with the congregation.

  • Delivery—believers remain seated and receive the elements from a tray passed down their row and consume the elements with the congregation in unison.

It is important to recognize that each of these means of distribution involves various points of delivery where the distinction between serving and passing gets fuzzy.

For instance, if a congregation uses the Dine-in method, does the distribution and division of the elements down the table through the hands of non-ordained members constitute serving or passing? If this act counts as passing, what distinguishes it from a non-ordained member delivering a tray to the end of a pew?

Or, if a congregation uses the Delivery method and a non-ordained person hands the elements to the person next to them, does this count as serving or passing? What distinguishes the act of delivering a tray to the end of a pew from delivering it to the next person on your pew? Or, what if a member shares a spoken word regarding Christ’s sacrifice with his neighbor as he passes the elements to him? Is this passing or serving?

This raises a series of questions that call the distinction between serving and passing into question. Where does serving end and passing begin? At what point does the act transform from one to the other? Is serving connected to a spoken word delivered with the sacramental elements? Or is serving bound up with optics and perception flowing from the front of the sanctuary?

In the end, the lack of clarity between serving and passing undermines the usefulness of the overture because the distinction produces more confusion than clarity.

Recommendation for Distribution

In our tumultuous moment, it is helpful to return to historical practices, not to slavishly repeat the past, but to learn from the wisdom of previous generations. To that end, John Knox’s order for observing the Lord’s Supper is a liturgical masterpiece that deserves our attention.

In the liturgy, the presiding minister delivers the WORDS OF INSTITUTION and EXHORTATION from the pulpit and then takes a seat with the congregation at a common table. After offering a lengthy PRAYER OF THANKSGIVING, the rubric in the liturgy reads:

This done, the minister breaks the bread and delivers it to the people, who distribute and divide the same among themselves, according to our Savior Christ’s commandment, and likewise gives the cup. During which time, some place of the Scriptures is read, which sets forth the death of Christ in a lively way, to the intent that our eyes and senses may not only be occupied in these outward signs of bread and wine, which are called the visible word, but that our hearts and minds also may be fully fixed in the contemplation of the Lord’s death, which is by this Holy Sacrament represented.

Let’s consider Knox’s twofold distinction: (1) the delivery of the consecrated elements by the presiding minister to the people and (2) the distribution and division of the elements among the people by the people. Significantly, after the presiding minister gives thanks and delivers the elements to the people, Knox assigns the distribution and division to them. In allowing believers to divide the elements among themselves, Knox indicates that this mode of distribution is in obedience to Christ’s commandment (Luke 22:17). Therefore, Knox does not connect the means of distribution to the keys of the kingdom through the ordained officers but connects it to a Scriptural commandment that democratizes the action.

Additionally, it is important to note that the focus, in Chapter 22 of the Scots Confession, is upon a lawfully ordained minister administering the Lord’s Supper, not the elders controlling the distribution of the elements around the table (pace Overture 60). For Knox, the distribution and division of the elements is a matter of sharing the spoils in keeping with Jesus’ appointment, not a flex of ecclesiastical authority.

This seems wise and judicious. To claim a necessary connection between the details of the distribution and the keys of the kingdom is a bridge too far. This goes well beyond Scripture into a level of micro-management that is imprecise and unhelpful.

Conclusion

Perhaps one reason Knox was not preoccupied with the distribution is that he focused his liturgy on the act of thanksgiving and creating a warm evangelical ethos around the table that was aimed to fix hearts and minds on Jesus Christ. For the sake of our own renewal and unity, we would do well to focus our denominational attention on thanksgiving and the Christ-centered ethos that Knox sought to nurture around the Lord’s Table, and not the minutiae of dubious distinctions.

Chuck Colson is the Lead Pastor of ChristChurch Presbyterian in Atlanta and serves as a Visiting Lecturer of Pastoral Theology at RTS, Orlando. He received his Ph.D. in Systematic Theology from the University of Aberdeen.
